title: Zulip User Guide
text:
Zulip Structure & Interaction
Zulip organises conversations into channels (listed with a globe icon on the left-hand side of the app/webpage) (Fig. 1A). Each of these covers a broad theme. The Palaeoverse Public Workspace is formed from eight channels:

Events
Funding
Jobs
Publications
Resources
Community
Help
Announcements

As a guest user, you will be able to post in the first seven of these (all channels bar “Announcements”), and interact with all of them. These channels were established by Palaeoverse administrators, and will remain constant. Although you won’t personally be able to create a new channel, we will consider any requests, and you should contact the administrators if you wish to add something new.




Figure 1: Channels and topics in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.



Within each channel, conversations are organised into topics (Fig. 1B). This means that many discussions can happen simultaneously within the same channel, and everyone can respond in their own time without the feed becoming confusing. To view the existing topics, just click on the channel you are interested in. When you want to start up a new conversation or post about an opportunity, you should create a new topic as follows (Fig. 2):

Choose a relevant channel.
Click the “start a new topic” button (square with a plus symbol inside) located next to the channel name.
Enter the topic name (see below on how this should be formatted).
Compose your message relating to the topic in the text box. If you would like to, you can preview your message before it is sent using the eye symbol.
Click the “send” button (arrow shaped).





Figure 2: Composing topics and messages in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.



Once a topic is created, all users will be able to respond to this. When you start composing a response, it will automatically be addressed to the topic that you are reading or have clicked on. This will be confirmed in the textbox with the text: Message #Channel Name > Topic Name (Fig. 3). If your message is posted in the wrong place, it may be moved by administrators. Don’t worry if this happens, it is just to keep the space organised!




Figure 3: Responding to topics in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.

title: Zulip User Guide
text:
Topic templates
To keep channels easy to navigate, we have provided channel-specific templates that should aim to be used when starting a new topic. These are provided below.

Events
The Palaeoverse Zulip workspace welcomes event (e.g. conference and workshop) advertisements on the themes of palaeontology and open science, as well as other relevant themes such as ecology and conservation science.
Topics posted within the Events channel should aim to take the full name of the event being advertised, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters (Zulip-imposed limit).
The initial post within the topic thread should try to take the following format, or similar:

Event name (in bold):
Location:
Dates:
Additional Details (if applicable):
Link to the conference web page:

All other information (e.g. registration reminders, circular updates) and discussion relating to a specific conference or workshop should be posted below the relevant topic.


Publications
Relevant publications on the themes of phylogenetics, palaeobiogeography, palaeoecology, palaeoclimate, diversity dynamics, geometric morphometrics, statistical analyses, conservation, open science, etc., should be posted here.
Topics within the Publications channel should take the full title of the paper, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters.
The initial post within the topic should aim to take the following format, or similar:

APA-format citation (in bold):
DOI link:
Abstract/Additional Details:

All discussion relating to the research paper should be posted below the relevant topic.


Jobs
The Palaeoverse Zulip workspace welcomes relevant job advertisements in the fields of palaeontology, ecology, open science, conservation science, etc. Academic employment opportunities should include PhD positions, even if these are technically studentships.
Topics within the Jobs channel should aim to take the job title and hiring institution, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters.
The initial post within the topic should try to take the following format, or similar:

Job title (in bold):
Location:
Hours:
Salary:
Closing Date:
Additional Details:
Link to the job web page:

Any other information relating to a specific job should be posted below the relevant topic.


Funding
The Palaeoverse Zulip workspace welcomes all relevant funding advertisements. Grant opportunities are encouraged for all career stages, and can target both academic and non-academic audiences.
Topics within the Funding channel should aim to take the grant name and funding body being advertised, but shortened versions will be allowed if the title length exceeds 60 characters.
The initial post within the topic should try take the following format, or similar:

Grant title (in bold):
Awarding body:
Closing Date:
Additional Details:
Link to application page:

Any other information relating to the funding opportunity should be posted below the relevant topic.


Resources
The Resources channel is broad in its scope. Posts are welcomed on topics such as websites, books, talks, and course materials. As the breadth of subjects posted here cover a wider range, no specific post template is provided; however, the topic title should remain short and descriptive.
All discussion relating to the advertised resource should be posted in the relevant topic thread.


Community
The Community channel is also broad in its scope. This is a place to share things such as surveys, open nominations for awards, competitions, society news, or other community-focused topics. As the subjects posted here could be highly variable in nature, no specific post template is provided; however, the topic title should remain short and descriptive. All discussion relating to the post should be written in the relevant topic thread.


Help
The Help channel can be used for questions relating to the topics of palaeontology, ecology, open science, conservation science, etc. As the breadth of subjects posted here will cover quite a wide range, no template is provided; however, the topic title should remain short and descriptive.
All responses to questions should be placed in the relevant topic thread.


Announcements
Posts within the Announcements channel will be used for announcements relating to the workspace, e.g. changes in operation, code of conduct, and wider user messages. These messages will only be permitted from members and administrators; however, as a user you will be able to interact with these.

Reporting Misconduct
When using the Palaeoverse Zulip Public Workspace, it is important to act in a way that is conducive to a positive and enriching environment. If you discover any instances of unacceptable behaviour that do not align with this ethos (as laid out in our Code of Conduct), we request that you report the incident as follows (Fig. 4):

Hover over the problematic message to reveal the three dots icon on the right.
Select “report message”.
Fill out the requested information. Moderators (Zulip Administrators and Owner) will see the message you’re reporting when they review your report and follow the protocol outlined in our Code of Conduct.
Click “Submit” to send.




Figure 4: Reporting a message in the Palaeoverse Zulip workspace.

title: Zulip User Guide
text:
Credit/Attribution for Shared Work

Published work
When sharing work (e.g. published papers, artwork) the appropriate credit should always be provided in the same post if it is not immediately obvious who the work can be attributed to.
Example 1: a post with a link to a paper does not need to be accompanied by any additional text as all accreditations (e.g. authors and publisher) are made clear within the link.
Example 2: a post comprising a single illustration file should be accompanied by additional text to provide accreditation.


Unpublished work
Unpublished data should not be posted unless there is explicit approval from its creator/owner. It is important to remember that all posts in the public channels can be viewed by anybody with access to the internet.

Open the compose box for a message.

Click the “add global time” clock icon beneath the box.

Select your intended Universal Time using the date and time picker.

Click Confirm to insert the time code into your message.

title: About us
text:
Palaeoverse is a community-driven initiative advancing open science in palaeontology through shared tools, training, and resources.
Founded in 2022 by Lewis A. Jones, Palaeoverse grew out of a simple but widespread frustration: palaeontologists were independently reinventing the same workflows. Without standard tools or protocols for cleaning and preparing data, duplicated effort was the norm and reproducibility suffered. A group of early-career researchers decided to do something about it.
The result was the palaeoverse R package, a toolkit designed to streamline data preparation and exploration for palaeontological research. What began as a pragmatic solution to a shared problem has since grown into something larger: a formally organised initiative spanning a full software ecosystem, hands-on training workshops, community resources, and spaces for researchers at all career stages to connect and collaborate.



Members of the Palaeoverse team meeting in London in April 2026. From left to right: Lewis A. Jones, William Gearty, Joseph Flannery-Sutherland, Erin Dillon, Bethany Allen, Cecily Nicholl, Etienne Bacher.

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Thanks for stopping by! Looking to find out how you can contribute to Palaeoverse? You have come to the right place!
We very much appreciate and encourage community contributions. Your contributions help shape and improve Palaeoverse packages to address community needs. Contributing is also a great way to build your coding and computational skills, share your expertise, and expand your research network. Contributions are recognized in a variety of ways, including in documentation files and on the Palaeoverse website, depending on the nature of the contribution.
If there is anything that is unclear within this guide, please let us know via Zulip, email, or by logging an issue so we can improve it.
There are multiple ways to contribute to Palaeoverse. This page will go through each of them, from engaging with the community to contributing code.

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Joining the community on Zulip
Zulip is where the community gathers to exchange and share useful resources, such as publications, job postings, event announcements, and tutorials, as well as have interesting discussions. Anyone can join this community.

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Sharing knowledge and resources
In addition to participating on Zulip, you can also share knowledge or resources by presenting in our monthly lecture series, or suggesting additions to our list of resources.
More generally, if you are interested in what we do, feel free to reach out at info@palaeoverse.org.
The remaining sections will focus on the software components of Palaeoverse. Engaging in these subsequent steps requires having a GitHub account (more information here).

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Logging or discussing GitHub issues
Code-oriented tasks that need working on are logged as Github ‘issues’ within the respective Palaeoverse GitHub repositories (e.g. current rphylopic issues can be found at github.com/palaeoverse/rphylopic). If you find a bug in our code, or want to request a new function or feature, this is the best place to document it. Here you can also discuss outstanding issues, including helping us to prioritise tasks (even adding an emoji in support or protest to an issue is useful).

title: Contribute to Palaeoverse
text:
Contributing to code or documentation
If you want to get involved with contributing code or documentation to our packages (e.g. fix a bug or improve a vignette) but don’t know where to start, you can begin by browsing the outstanding issues. Once you find an issue that you want to address, we ask that you add a message in the issue to let people know that you are working on it.
If you are just getting started with collaborative coding, we recommend looking for issues labelled ‘Good First Issue’. These issues are relatively small and/or simple in scope, and are less of a time commitment than larger feature requests. Feel free to find an unclaimed ‘Good First Issue’ that interests you, ‘claim’ it by adding a comment to it, and jump in!
The section below presents an overview of the process to contribute code, but we also have a more detailed guide to explain the entire process, from installing required tools to submitting your changes in a pull request.

Contribution workflow (pull request process)
The contribution workflow below requires you to have basic knowledge of git and Github. If this is not the case, you can reach out to one of the core team members via email and they can make a pull request on your behalf, or help to guide you through the pull request and review process. However, you will be expected to respond to any reviewer comments on GitHub yourself (see below).
To make a pull request:

You (the contributor) should fork the repository (e.g. for the palaeoverse R package)

Clone the desired repository to your personal computer

Create a new git branch for your modifications (you should not make changes directly on the main branch)

Make your changes

Commit your changes (make sure your commit message is informative and concise)

Push your commits to your forked repository

When your changes are complete, you should submit them for merging via a pull request (“PR”) on GitHub

Note that a complete pull request should include a succinct description of what the code changes do, proper documentation (via roxygen2), and unit tests (via testthat). Only the description is required for the initial pull request and code review (see below), but pull requests will not be merged until they contain complete documentation and tests.
You also have to ensure that you follow our AI policy.


Minor changes
You can fix typos, spelling mistakes, or grammatical errors in function documentation and vignettes directly on GitHub (note that Github will automatically create a fork for you). However, note that fixing typos in the function documentation (those in the “Reference” page on the package website) requires editing the source in the corresponding .R file and then running devtools::document(). Do not manually edit an .Rd file in the man folder.


Substantial changes
If you would like to make a substantial change (e.g. add a new argument to an existing function or create a new function), you should first file an issue and make sure someone from the development team agrees that it’s needed (this prevents potentially wasted effort).
If you’ve found a bug, please file an issue that illustrates the bug with a reproducible example. The reprex package is very useful to build a minimal reproducible example.


The life of a pull request
Submitting a pull request for one of Palaeoverse’s R packages will automatically initiate several checks via GitHub Actions, such as R CMD check, linting and formatting checks, and test coverage check (among others). These checks will conduct some automatic review to ensure the new code doesn’t break any existing functionality and follows code standards.
Once these automated checks pass, at least two members of the Palaeoverse core team will manually review the changes before merging the pull request. This review should happen within a few days of opening a pull request. Note that if your pull request is not complete, it should be converted to draft.
Submitting a pull request is a big step, but it rarely happens that a pull request can be merged as-is. Like during the peer-review process for a journal article, reviewers will have questions and comments that you will need to address via the GitHub interface. If fixes and/or changes are required, you are expected to make these changes. Handling reviewers’ feedback might not be easy and can even feel adversarial sometimes, but remember that everyone has the same objective: producing good quality software. The Tidyteam code review guide is a great resource to understand better what is expected from you during code review and how reviewers will assess your code.

title: Mentorship Scheme
text:
What is the Mentorship Scheme?
Through the Palaeoverse Mentorship Scheme, you will upskill from software user to creator across six months of online learning, working alongside a cohort of early career researchers and under the mentorship of experienced Palaeoverse members. You will learn best practices for coding and package design in the R programming language as well as how to manage a software development project from start to finish. The scheme will culminate in code contributions to the Palaeoverse software ecosystem, and will deliver transferable data science skills that you can apply in your own research. There will also be opportunities to develop your own teaching skills at future in-person Palaeoverse workshops, hackathons and conference events.
By the scheme’s end, you will become a champion for open science, open-source tools, and reproducibility in palaeobiology. You will be able to implement robust data science workflows in R more efficiently, and will gain the skills to design and publish new software collaboratively to a professional standard. You will also be primed to convey these skills to your peers, setting you up for continued success in academic or industry settings.
Detailed information on the Palaeoverse Mentorship Scheme can be found below. If you have a question that is not addressed fully, or want to discuss your application with us, then please reach out on social media or via email info@palaeoverse.org. You can also join our community platform on Zulip and ask questions in the Community channel.

title: Mentorship Scheme
text:
Who is the scheme for?
The scheme is intended for early career researchers who currently use R in their work, and who wish to advance their coding ability and develop skills in collaborative software development and open science. We anticipate that it will be most beneficial to MSc/PhD students or recent doctoral graduates with a reasonable foundation in R, but who have little to no prior experience with GitHub workflows, package development, or contributing to open-source projects. The scheme is targeted towards software development for palaeobiology, therefore an undergraduate or master’s degree in palaeobiology or a related discipline (geology, evolutionary biology, etc.) will benefit your application.
The scheme is not intended as an introduction to R programming, nor will other programming languages be directly addressed. Applicants should be comfortable with most or all of the following:

importing and manipulating simple data in R
working with basic R data structures (e.g. vectors, data frames, lists)
writing and running their own scripts, or a script written by someone else
installing R packages and using their functions

We seek to widen the diversity of people involved in open science, especially in palaeobiology, via our mentee cohorts. We therefore actively encourage applications from underrepresented groups in the palaeobiology, open science, and software development communities.

title: Mentorship Scheme
text:
How does the scheme work?
The Palaeoverse Mentorship Scheme will be run online over six months. All content will be delivered in English using the digital platforms Github, Zoom and Zulip. Live sessions will take place at the start of each month, with the time zone to be decided based on the geographic composition of the cohort. Months 1–2: Modules in scripting, function design and data science
Month 3: First code contribution

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Introduction
While you can make plots with just the packages that come bundled with base R, many R users make their visualizations entirely using the ggplot2 package and an ecosystem of packages designed around it.

# load the ggplot2 package
library(ggplot2)

To demonstrate this, we’ll be using the Palmer penguins dataset (built-in to R as of version 4.5.0). First, let’s load the dataset. Then let’s inspect the data using the glimpse() function.

data(penguins)
dplyr::glimpse(penguins)

Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species     <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island      <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Tor…
$ bill_len    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, 42.0, …
$ bill_dep    <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, 20.2, …
$ flipper_len <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186, 180,…
$ body_mass   <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250, …
$ sex         <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male, NA, …
$ year        <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…


This dataset includes many different measurements for individual penguins from three different studies. The studies cover both sexes of three different species of penguins from three different islands in the Palmer Archipelago.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
The ggplot2 basics
The most important function in the ggplot2 package is ggplot(). Note that this function doesn’t include the “2” of the package name. Let’s go ahead and try using this function on our penguins data.

ggplot(penguins)








You’ll notice that the ggplot() function doesn’t actually do much by itself. Here, we provide it with the penguins dataset, but the result looks like someone started making a plot and then stopped after the first step of making the rectangle for the plot area. This is because ggplot2 is designed around the “grammar of graphics”. Therefore, it expects you to build a sentence-like structure out of its functions. A single word (i.e., the call to ggplot() above) doesn’t make much of a sentence, so let’s start building up a real sentence.
By using the ggplot() function, we are essentially stating that we are beginning a plotting “sentence”. We then combine this with other “words” (function calls) using the + operator. The next component you usually want to specify in a ggplot “sentence” is our “aesthetic” mappings. These specify the columns of the dataset that correspond to each axis of the plot, including the x/y axes, but also the axes of color, shape, etc. We do this with the aes() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len)








Hey, it’s starting to look like a plot now! Except there isn’t any actual data being plotted. Let’s fix that. We’ll start off with a simple scatter plot by using the geom_point() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point()








And there we go! You’ll notice that with just a few lines, we’ve already made a pretty nice visualization of this penguin data. ggplot2 does most of the work for us once we specify our dataset and our x and y variables.






NoteMissing data



You may have noticed a warning that some rows of the dataset contain missing values. There are two penguins without any measurements in the dataset. How might we remove them using dplyr so we don’t get this warning over and over?






CautionSolution






penguins <- penguins |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass))






Now, let’s go a step further and color the points by another variable (e.g., the island of the penguins). With ggplot2, all that requires is specifying another aesthetic:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point()








Notice that ggplot2 comes with its own default color scheme. However, I would strongly discourage you from using the default colors, especially as the number of categories increases (with only 3 categories here it isn’t too bad). Let’s try out some of the more accessible color palettes that are also available in R.
First, let’s try one of the viridis color palettes. Since this palette is included in ggplot2, all we need to do is add the proper “scale” to our ggplot() call. Scales tell ggplot how to handle a particular aesthetic, and are usually of the form scale_[aesthetic]_[type]().

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) # avoid yellow at the end of the palette








Now let’s try one of the brewer color palettes.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")








Outside of color, there are many other aspects of the graph that we can modify using aesthetics and “scale”s. For example, we can modify the shape of the points:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")














NoteMore missing data



Urgh, more missing data! It appears that nine of the penguins are missing sex identification data. We can ignore the warning message, but that extra “NA” category in the legend is quite annoying. We can remove this category from the legend using na.translate = FALSE within scale_shape_discrete() (you could also use scale_shape_manual() if you wanted to supply your own shapes):

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE)










And the x/y axes:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)")

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Theming
The last basic thing you might want to do with ggplot2 is modify the style of the visualization. This is extremely customizable, but the first place to start is with a built-in theme. I personally prefer the classic theme, which looks very similar to base R plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic()








Using this built-in theme has changed many visual aspects of the graph, including changing the plot background color, adding axis lines, and removing the internal grid lines. If you look very closely, however, the axis tick labels are still a slight grey. We can use the theme() function to further customize the appearance and change this. In this case, we’ll make the axis text elements have a black color instead of the default gray.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








And there we have it! With just 10 lines we’ve created what I would say is a publication quality graph! ggplot does a lot of the tedious work for us, giving us time to focus on the more important aspects, such as labeling and color. Admittedly, I’ve spent a LOT of time on these aspects in the past…
More information about all of the hierarchical theme components that you can customize is available here. In order to change many of these components, you need to use theme elements like we did above with element_text(). That and other theme elements are documented here.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
More complex features

Other layers
There are many other types of plots that we can make with ggplot2.

Histograms
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable with a histogram:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














Note



Histograms don’t require a y-axis aesthetic by default. The counts are tabulated for you. If you specify a “fill” aesthetic, the default is to stack the bars which can sometimes be a bit misleading. You can also dodge them to fix this:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram(position = "dodge") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))












Boxplots and Violin Plotss
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable across a discrete variable with boxplots or violin plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))









ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", draw_quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteGeom options



Note that many of these “geom”s have lots of options. For example, here we’ve decided to scale all of the violin plots to the same width and to draw the quartiles on them (mimicking the boxplots above). You can see all of the options for a geom by checking out it’s help page (?geom_violin) or on the ggplot website.




2D Contours
We can also visualize the density of values across two continuous variables using a 2D contour:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Note that sometimes you may need to expand the axes a little bit to better show the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12.5, NA)) + # NA means "don't change"
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))










Time Series
Since there isn’t really any time series data in the penguins dataset, we’ll take a quick detour and use the built-in economics dataset to explore visualizing a time series. In this case, we are looking at unemployment over time:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








geom_path() lets you explore how two variables are related over time. For example, unemployment and personal savings rate:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = unemploy / pop, y = psavert)) +
  geom_path(aes(colour = as.numeric(date))) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteMultiple columns for individual aesthetics



Note how we’ve used multiple columns of the data to define the x-axis here. You can use any sort of mathematical operators to combine multiple columns into a single aesthetic, as long as you are doing row-wise math.





Combining layers
We can also combine multiple layers to show the same data in different ways in the same plot. For example, we could show the raw data for the above contour plot in addition to the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + # don't expand the axes so the background is all filled
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteLayer order



When combining layers, the layers are added to the plot in order, so in this case the points are the bottom layer and the contour lines are the top layer. We changed the alpha of the middle layer to prevent the points from being blocked. I’ve also used the coord_cartesian() function to remove the default axis expansion. This way the background color reaches both axes and doesn’t have a white gap.




Facetting
Let’s take our scatterplot example from earlier:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Now, what if we wanted to also split the data by the species of the penguins? We’re already using color and shape, so what other aesthetic could we use? We could possible use some shapes that have both a fill and outline color, but that sounds messy. Instead of using another aesthetic, we could also use a facet. This splits the chart into multiple panels:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(species), ncol = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








We can get even crazier by faceting by multiple variables:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(species), cols = vars(year)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








OK, maybe we’ve gone a little too far here, but you get the picture!

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Combining plots
When publishing results, often we need to combine multiple figures into a single visualization. There are lots of packages for accomplishing this (even my own deeptime package has some functionality for it), but today we’ll check out the patchwork package which extends the “grammar of graphics” to combining plots (you may need to install it if you haven’t done so already).

library(patchwork)

First, let’s go ahead and make some plots. Instead of plotting them, though, we’ll save them as objects in our environment. Note that when you save a plot to an object it isn’t displayed in the “Plots” tab.

g1 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

g2 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

Now, in order to combine these, all we need to do is combine them using the + operator, like we did with the individual elements of the plots.

g1 + g2








You can see that patchwork does all of the work for us, lining up the different components of the plots. If we have more plots to combine, we can then use the | (side-by-side) and / (above-and-below) operators to make more complex arrangements of plots.

g3 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

(g1 | g2) / g3








There’s a lot more you can do with patchwork, including adjusting the widths and heights and adding annotations and styling, but we’ll stop here for now.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Saving plots
The last big thing you’ll need to know about plotting is how to save your plots. ggplot2 comes with a nifty ggsave() function which you can use to save your plots in a number of different formats. Here we’ll save our most recent combined plot as both a PDF and a JPEG. The former is a vector format, meaning all of the elements of the figure as geometric shapes, and, because of this, none of the data is lost (aka “lossless”). The latter is a raster format, meaning the figure is converted to a 2-D array of colored pixels of a desired size, and because of this, some of the data is lost in the process (aka “lossy”). This results in the pixellation that you see when you zoom in on a JPEG. ggsave() detects what format you want based on the file extension, so we just need to specify the file location and the object to be saved (and optionally the dimensions of the output file). It’s usually a good idea to keep all figures in their own folder (which was already created for you).

gg <- (g1 | g2) / g3
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.pdf", gg, height = 10, width = 10)
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.jpg", gg, height = 10, width = 10)

The last big thing you’ll need to know about plotting is how to save your plots. ggplot2 comes with a nifty ggsave() function which you can use to save your plots in a number of different formats. Here we’ll save our most recent combined plot as both a PDF and a JPEG. The former is a vector format, meaning all of the elements of the figure as geometric shapes, and, because of this, none of the data is lost (aka “lossless”). The latter is a raster format, meaning the figure is converted to a 2-D array of colored pixels of a desired size, and because of this, some of the data is lost in the process (aka “lossy”). ggsave("figures/penguins_1.jpg", gg, height = 10, width = 10)

text:
Objectives

Learn the essential steps to debug R code
Learn how to use the package reprex to create a small reproducible example
Learn how to use specific debugging tools such as browser() and breakpoints

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Introduction
Knowing how to debug code is an essential skill, whether one writes an analysis for a paper or develops an R package. This module covers several tools that aim to make the debugging process easier.




The following code is taken from the “Latitudinal trends in Phanerozoic reefs” vignette, but let’s pretend we have written this code from scratch:

library(palaeoverse)

data(reefs)
reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
# Assign a common time scale based on an interval key
reefs <- look_up(occdf = reefs,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)
reefs <- subset(reefs, interval_max_ma <= 541)
# Extract Phanerozoic stage-level stages for time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs, bins = bins, method = "mid")

Error in `[.data.frame`:
! undefined columns selected


We now have an error, but its cause is not immediately clear. Therefore, we’ll have to do some debugging.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
section: Reduce the size of the data
text:
Reduce the size of the data
In the debugging process, we will likely run the code at least a handful of times. Therefore, we want to make sure that it runs as fast as possible so that we don’t lose our focus. The easiest way to do this is to reduce the size of our input data.
In addition to making the error appear faster, it is also easier to compare the actual and expected outputs when the data is as small as possible.
In this example, the dataset we are using has thousands of rows and 14 columns:

dim(reefs)

[1] 4335   19


Let’s try to reduce the size of our data:

reefs2 <- head(reefs)

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
# Assign a common time scale based on an interval key
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)
reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)
# Extract Phanerozoic stage-level stages for time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

Error in `[.data.frame`:
! undefined columns selected


We still see the same error but now we only have 6 rows left, much better! Let’s try to reduce that to one row and to remove some columns.

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:5]

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)

Error in `group_apply()`:
! Supplied `group` is not a named column in `occdf`

# Assign a common time scale based on an interval key
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)

Error in `look_up()`:
! `early_interval` needs to match a column name of `occdf`

reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)

Error:
! object 'interval_max_ma' not found

# Extract Phanerozoic stage-level stages for time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

Error in `[.data.frame`:
! undefined columns selected


Hmm, we don’t have the same error anymore, so we removed too many columns. Let’s try to keep 6 instead of 5:

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
# Assign a common time scale based on an interval key
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)
reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)
# Extract Phanerozoic stage-level stages for time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

Error in `[.data.frame`:
! undefined columns selected


Bingo! We have the same error as before, but now we only have one row and six columns.
Let’s now try to reduce the size of the code.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
section: Reduce the size of the code
text:
Reduce the size of the code
This is an important process: we want to remove as much code as possible to lower the number of potential causes leading to the error.
Starting from this:

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
# Assign a common time scale based on an interval key
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)
reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)
# Extract Phanerozoic stage-level stages for time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

Error in `[.data.frame`:
! undefined columns selected


We see that reef_counts is defined but never actually used, so this cannot be the root cause. Let’s remove it.
The subset() call is also suspicious: now that he have only one row left in our test data, does this subset() actually do anything?

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)

identical(reefs2, subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541))

[1] TRUE


It doesn’t affect reefs2, so let’s remove it as well.
We now have this:

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

Error in `[.data.frame`:
! undefined columns selected


We have removed two out of five function calls, not bad. We still don’t really understand the cause though.
Let’s assume that the documentation also doesn’t give any hint about this error message. If we are completely stuck, then we may want to ask other people, such as package maintainers on Github or people on StackOverflow. We have done our best to reduce the size of the problem, making it easier for other people to help us.
Still, we need to ensure that our reprex is correctly made and we must find a nice way to share it.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
browser()
The bug report above gives a reprex to reproduce the error (note that at the time you are reading this, this bug has already been fixed):

library(palaeoverse)

occdf <- reefs[1:5, ]
bin_space(occdf = occdf, spacing = 1000, sub_grid = 250, return = TRUE)

Error in `bin_space()`:
! object 'secondary' not found


The error happens in bin_space(), which is a long function:
palaeoverse::bin_space
#> function (occdf, lng = "lng", lat = "lat", spacing = 100, sub_grid = NULL, 
#>     return = FALSE, plot = FALSE) 
#> {
#>     if (!is.data.frame(occdf)) {
#>         stop("occdf should be of class dataframe")
#>     }
#>    
#>    [ MANUALLY TRUNCATED ]
#>   
#> }
One approach to narrow down the cause of the error would be to add multiple print() statements, so that we can check which messages are printed (indicating that the code ran without error) and which are not because the error occurred before reaching them.
However, it would be way more convenient to be able to execute the internal code line by line so that we can see precisely which line errors. This is the objective of browser(). We can start by putting a browser() at the top, re-load the function, and execute it again:
function (occdf, lng = "lng", lat = "lat", spacing = 100, sub_grid = NULL, 
    return = FALSE, plot = FALSE) 
{
+   browser()  
    if (!is.data.frame(occdf)) {
        stop("occdf should be of class dataframe")
    }
   
   [ MANUALLY TRUNCATED ]
  
}
In the video below, running the code with the function that now includes browser() doesn’t error. Instead, it stops the execution at the browser() call:
Video
There are two interesting things in this video:

we have access to the function environment, including the user-provided inputs. Note for instance that sub_grid is NULL by default in the function definition, but printing sub_grid in the console gives 250 because the call that is being inspected contains sub_grid = 250.
We can execute the remaining function body statement by statement by pressing “Enter” in the console. Note that this goes doesn’t necessarily execute all the code: an if() statement whose condition is FALSE will not be executed. browser() follows exactly the path taken by our code.

Pressing “Esc” or executing Q allows us to exit this “browsing” mode.
Using this approach, we can find the exact source of the error:
Video
In our case, the error comes from the line:
occdf <- list(occdf, grid, base_grid, primary, secondary)
Fixing this requires reading all the code prior to this line, but this is out of scope for this blog post.
If you are confident that some lines are irrelevant to the bug, you can move the browser() call past them so that you don’t need to execute them all every time you enter “browsing” mode.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Breakpoints
Breakpoints are a feature directly integrated in the software used to run R (e.g. RStudio or Positron. This is also known as IDE for “Integrated Development Environment”).
They are a way to mimic browser() calls without actually modifying the function. You can add one by clicking on the left of line numbers:
Video
After reloading the package and running the code that is supposed to fail, we end up in almost the same situation as with browser(), except that we haven’t modified the source code at all. We can then follow the same steps to continue our debugging process.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Theming

The last basic thing you might want to do with ggplot2 is modify the style of the visualization. This is extremely customizable, but the first place to start is with a built-in theme. I personally prefer the classic theme, which looks very similar to base R plots:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic()

text:
Histograms

We can visualize the density of values for a single variable with a histogram:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Boxplots and Violin Plotss

We can visualize the density of values for a single variable across a discrete variable with boxplots or violin plots:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
2D Contours

We can also visualize the density of values across two continuous variables using a 2D contour:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Time Series

Since there isn’t really any time series data in the penguins dataset, we’ll take a quick detour and use the built-in economics dataset to explore visualizing a time series. In this case, we are looking at unemployment over time:


ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Combining layers

We can also combine multiple layers to show the same data in different ways in the same plot. For example, we could show the raw data for the above contour plot in addition to the contours:


ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + # don't expand the axes so the background is all filled
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

Let’s take our scatterplot example from earlier:

      color = island, shape = sex) +

  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +

  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +

text:
Introduction
While you can make plots with just the packages that come bundled with base R, many R users make their visualizations entirely using the ggplot2 package and an ecosystem of packages designed around it.

# load the ggplot2 package
library(ggplot2)

To demonstrate this, we’ll be using the Palmer penguins dataset (built-in to R as of version 4.5.0). First, let’s load the dataset. Then let’s inspect the data using the glimpse() function.

data(penguins)
dplyr::glimpse(penguins)

Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species     <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island      <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Tor…
$ bill_len    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, 42.0, …
$ bill_dep    <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, 20.2, …
$ flipper_len <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186, 180,…
$ body_mass   <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250, …
$ sex         <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male, NA, …
$ year        <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…


This dataset includes many different measurements for individual penguins from three different studies. The studies cover both sexes of three different species of penguins from three different islands in the Palmer Archipelago.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
The ggplot2 basics
The most important function in the ggplot2 package is ggplot(). Note that this function doesn’t include the “2” of the package name. Let’s go ahead and try using this function on our penguins data.

ggplot(penguins)








You’ll notice that the ggplot() function doesn’t actually do much by itself. Here, we provide it with the penguins dataset, but the result looks like someone started making a plot and then stopped after the first step of making the rectangle for the plot area. This is because ggplot2 is designed around the “grammar of graphics”. Therefore, it expects you to build a sentence-like structure out of its functions. A single word (i.e., the call to ggplot() above) doesn’t make much of a sentence, so let’s start building up a real sentence.
By using the ggplot() function, we are essentially stating that we are beginning a plotting “sentence”. We then combine this with other “words” (function calls) using the + operator. The next component you usually want to specify in a ggplot “sentence” is our “aesthetic” mappings. These specify the columns of the dataset that correspond to each axis of the plot, including the x/y axes, but also the axes of color, shape, etc. We do this with the aes() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len)








Hey, it’s starting to look like a plot now! Except there isn’t any actual data being plotted. Let’s fix that. We’ll start off with a simple scatter plot by using the geom_point() function:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point()








And there we go! You’ll notice that with just a few lines, we’ve already made a pretty nice visualization of this penguin data. ggplot2 does most of the work for us once we specify our dataset and our x and y variables.






NoteMissing data



You may have noticed a warning that some rows of the dataset contain missing values. There are two penguins without any measurements in the dataset. How might we remove them using dplyr so we don’t get this warning over and over?






CautionSolution






penguins <- penguins |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass))






Now, let’s go a step further and color the points by another variable (e.g., the island of the penguins). With ggplot2, all that requires is specifying another aesthetic:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point()








Notice that ggplot2 comes with its own default color scheme. However, I would strongly discourage you from using the default colors, especially as the number of categories increases (with only 3 categories here it isn’t too bad). Let’s try out some of the more accessible color palettes that are also available in R.
First, let’s try one of the viridis color palettes. Since this palette is included in ggplot2, all we need to do is add the proper “scale” to our ggplot() call. Scales tell ggplot how to handle a particular aesthetic, and are usually of the form scale_[aesthetic]_[type]().

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) # avoid yellow at the end of the palette








Now let’s try one of the brewer color palettes.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")








Outside of color, there are many other aspects of the graph that we can modify using aesthetics and “scale”s. For example, we can modify the shape of the points:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")














NoteMore missing data



Urgh, more missing data! It appears that nine of the penguins are missing sex identification data. We can ignore the warning message, but that extra “NA” category in the legend is quite annoying. We can remove this category from the legend using na.translate = FALSE within scale_shape_discrete() (you could also use scale_shape_manual() if you wanted to supply your own shapes):

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE)










And the x/y axes:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)")

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Theming
The last basic thing you might want to do with ggplot2 is modify the style of the visualization. This is extremely customizable, but the first place to start is with a built-in theme. I personally prefer the classic theme, which looks very similar to base R plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic()








Using this built-in theme has changed many visual aspects of the graph, including changing the plot background color, adding axis lines, and removing the internal grid lines. If you look very closely, however, the axis tick labels are still a slight grey. We can use the theme() function to further customize the appearance and change this. In this case, we’ll make the axis text elements have a black color instead of the default gray.

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island,
      shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








And there we have it! With just 10 lines we’ve created what I would say is a publication quality graph! ggplot does a lot of the tedious work for us, giving us time to focus on the more important aspects, such as labeling and color. Admittedly, I’ve spent a LOT of time on these aspects in the past…
More information about all of the hierarchical theme components that you can customize is available here. In order to change many of these components, you need to use theme elements like we did above with element_text(). That and other theme elements are documented here.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
More complex features

Other layers
There are many other types of plots that we can make with ggplot2.

Histograms
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable with a histogram:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














Note



Histograms don’t require a y-axis aesthetic by default. The counts are tabulated for you. If you specify a “fill” aesthetic, the default is to stack the bars which can sometimes be a bit misleading. You can also dodge them to fix this:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, fill = species) +
  geom_histogram(position = "dodge") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))












Boxplots and Violin Plotss
We can visualize the density of values for a single variable across a discrete variable with boxplots or violin plots:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))









ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", draw_quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteGeom options



Note that many of these “geom”s have lots of options. For example, here we’ve decided to scale all of the violin plots to the same width and to draw the quartiles on them (mimicking the boxplots above). You can see all of the options for a geom by checking out it’s help page (?geom_violin) or on the ggplot website.




2D Contours
We can also visualize the density of values across two continuous variables using a 2D contour:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Note that sometimes you may need to expand the axes a little bit to better show the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12.5, NA)) + # NA means "don't change"
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))










Time Series
Since there isn’t really any time series data in the penguins dataset, we’ll take a quick detour and use the built-in economics dataset to explore visualizing a time series. In this case, we are looking at unemployment over time:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








geom_path() lets you explore how two variables are related over time. For example, unemployment and personal savings rate:

ggplot(economics, aes(x = unemploy / pop, y = psavert)) +
  geom_path(aes(colour = as.numeric(date))) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteMultiple columns for individual aesthetics



Note how we’ve used multiple columns of the data to define the x-axis here. You can use any sort of mathematical operators to combine multiple columns into a single aesthetic, as long as you are doing row-wise math.





Combining layers
We can also combine multiple layers to show the same data in different ways in the same plot. For example, we could show the raw data for the above contour plot in addition to the contours:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + # don't expand the axes so the background is all filled
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))














NoteLayer order



When combining layers, the layers are added to the plot in order, so in this case the points are the bottom layer and the contour lines are the top layer. We changed the alpha of the middle layer to prevent the points from being blocked. I’ve also used the coord_cartesian() function to remove the default axis expansion. This way the background color reaches both axes and doesn’t have a white gap.




Facetting
Let’s take our scatterplot example from earlier:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








Now, what if we wanted to also split the data by the species of the penguins? We’re already using color and shape, so what other aesthetic could we use? We could possible use some shapes that have both a fill and outline color, but that sounds messy. Instead of using another aesthetic, we could also use a facet. This splits the chart into multiple panels:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(species), ncol = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








We can get even crazier by faceting by multiple variables:

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len,
      color = island, shape = sex) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_shape_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Body Mass (grams)") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (millimeters)") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(species), cols = vars(year)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))








OK, maybe we’ve gone a little too far here, but you get the picture!

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Combining plots
When publishing results, often we need to combine multiple figures into a single visualization. There are lots of packages for accomplishing this (even my own deeptime package has some functionality for it), but today we’ll check out the patchwork package which extends the “grammar of graphics” to combining plots (you may need to install it if you haven’t done so already).

library(patchwork)

First, let’s go ahead and make some plots. Instead of plotting them, though, we’ll save them as objects in our environment. Note that when you save a plot to an object it isn’t displayed in the “Plots” tab.

g1 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

g2 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density_2d(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(12, 23)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

Now, in order to combine these, all we need to do is combine them using the + operator, like we did with the individual elements of the plots.

g1 + g2








You can see that patchwork does all of the work for us, lining up the different components of the plots. If we have more plots to combine, we can then use the | (side-by-side) and / (above-and-below) operators to make more complex arrangements of plots.

g3 <- ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = island, y = bill_len) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

(g1 | g2) / g3








There’s a lot more you can do with patchwork, including adjusting the widths and heights and adding annotations and styling, but we’ll stop here for now.

title: Plotting in R with ggplot2
text:
Saving plots
The last big thing you’ll need to know about plotting is how to save your plots. ggplot2 comes with a nifty ggsave() function which you can use to save your plots in a number of different formats. Here we’ll save our most recent combined plot as both a PDF and a JPEG. The former is a vector format, meaning all of the elements of the figure as geometric shapes, and, because of this, none of the data is lost (aka “lossless”). The latter is a raster format, meaning the figure is converted to a 2-D array of colored pixels of a desired size, and because of this, some of the data is lost in the process (aka “lossy”). This results in the pixellation that you see when you zoom in on a JPEG. ggsave() detects what format you want based on the file extension, so we just need to specify the file location and the object to be saved (and optionally the dimensions of the output file). It’s usually a good idea to keep all figures in their own folder (which was already created for you).

gg <- (g1 | g2) / g3
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.pdf", gg, height = 10, width = 10)
ggsave("figures/penguins_1.jpg", gg, height = 10, width = 10)

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Objectives


Learn the essential steps to debug R code



Create a small reproducible example with reprex




Use browser() and breakpoints

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
A failing script

From the “Latitudinal trends in Phanerozoic reefs” vignette:

library(palaeoverse)

data(reefs)
reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
reefs <- look_up(occdf = reefs,
                 early_interval = "interval",
                 late_interval = "interval",
                 int_key = interval_key)
reefs <- subset(reefs, interval_max_ma <= 541)
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs, bins = bins, method = "mid")

#> Error in `[.data.frame`:
#> ! undefined columns selected

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Minimal reproducible example


Longer code = more potential causes.



First step: build a reproducible example, aka a reprex.




Two steps:

reduce the data
reduce the code

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the data

Smaller data:

runs faster
makes outputs easier to compare



Our dataset has thousands of rows and 14 columns:

library(palaeoverse)
dim(reefs)

[1] 4363   14

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the data

Keep only the first 6 rows:

reefs2 <- head(reefs)

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                  early_interval = "interval",
                  late_interval = "interval",
                  int_key = interval_key)
reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

#> Error in `[.data.frame`:
#> ! undefined columns selected

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the data

Keep one row and 5 columns:

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:5]

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)

Error in `group_apply()`:
! Supplied `group` is not a named column in `occdf`

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the data

Keep one row and 6 columns:

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                  early_interval = "interval",
                  late_interval = "interval",
                  int_key = interval_key)
reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

#> Error in `[.data.frame`:
#> ! undefined columns selected

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the code

Remove as much code as possible to limit potential causes.

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reef_counts <- group_apply(occdf = reefs2, group = "interval", fun = nrow)
reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                  early_interval = "interval",
                  late_interval = "interval",
                  int_key = interval_key)
reefs2 <- subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541)
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the code


reef_counts is never used: remove it.



Does subset() do anything with one row?


identical(reefs2, subset(reefs2, interval_max_ma <= 541))
#> [1] TRUE




No: remove it too.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Reduce the code

What we have now:

reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                  early_interval = "interval",
                  late_interval = "interval",
                  int_key = interval_key)
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")


Two out of five function calls removed, but still no clear cause.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Next step
 
Stuck? Ask for help (GitHub, StackOverflow, colleagues).


But before that…

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Clean the environment

Our session may contain objects and options unrelated to the problem.


They can interact with our code.



Restarting R works, but is easy to forget.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
reprex()

reprex::reprex() runs code in a separate, clean R session.



Errors if the code isn’t self-contained.




If it runs in reprex(), others can reproduce it.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
reprex()


reprex::reprex({
  reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
  reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

  reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                    early_interval = "interval",
                    late_interval = "interval",
                    int_key = interval_key)
  bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

  bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")
})


reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
#> Error:
#> ! object 'reefs' not found

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
reprex()


reprex::reprex({
  library(palaeoverse)
  data(reefs)
  reefs2 <- head(reefs, n = 1)
  reefs2 <- reefs2[, 1:6]

  reefs2 <- look_up(occdf = reefs2,
                    early_interval = "interval",
                    late_interval = "interval",
                    int_key = interval_key)
  bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")

  bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")
})


bin_time(occdf = reefs2, bins = bins, method = "mid")
#> Error in `[.data.frame`:
#> ! undefined columns selected

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
reprex()

Good practice: add session info with si = TRUE.

reprex::reprex({
  library(palaeoverse)
  ...
}, si = TRUE)



Reducing the problem is key, and often reveals the bug by itself.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Debugging a function

A function runs a whole block of code and only shows the final error.


One reflex: add print() statements.



Better: browser() pauses execution inside the function.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Example

Based on issue #280 in palaeoverse (now fixed):

library(palaeoverse)

occdf <- reefs[1:5, ]
bin_space(occdf = occdf, spacing = 1000, sub_grid = 250, return = TRUE)

Error in `bin_space()`:
! object 'secondary' not found


bin_space() is a long function: where does it fail?

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
browser()


We have access to the function environment.



E.g. sub_grid is 250, not its default NULL.




Press “Enter” to run the next statement.




Only the path actually taken is executed (e.g. no if (FALSE)).




Press “Esc” or run Q to exit.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
browser()

Step through until the code fails:

occdf <- list(occdf, grid, base_grid, primary, secondary)



Tip: move browser() past lines that are irrelevant.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Breakpoints

Built into IDEs like RStudio or Positron.


Click left of a line number to add one.



Same as browser(), without modifying the code.

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text: Breakpoints

title: Debugging with reprex() and browser()
text:
Conclusion


Reduce the data and the code.



Check your reprex with reprex().




Inspect functions with browser() and breakpoints.




Good debugging helps you fix your code and improves bug reports.
