title: Contribute to our packages
text: This page details the process to contribute code or documentation to one of our R packages. See the general guide to learn more ways to contribute to Palaeoverse.

title: Contribute to our packages
text:
Required tools
Besides R, you will need to use a variety of tools to ease the development process and to ensure that your contribution follows the Palaeoverse code standards.

R packages:

devtools: this contains many functions that make package development significantly easier

pak: this provides some functions to install all dependencies of the package you want to contribute to. It is good to install optional dependencies because some tests or examples will use them.

Other tools (see screenshots below):

Air: this is a code formatter, it ensures that all R code in the package follows a common style (e.g. it automatically adds whitespace or breaks lines where needed). You can install it from here: https://posit-dev.github.io/air/cli.html
You might need to restart RStudio (or the IDE that you use, if you use one) after installing it. This tool runs in the terminal, not the R console. You can check that it is correctly installed by running air -V to print its version number.
Jarl: this is a code linter, it checks R code to find common mistakes or programming patterns that shouldn’t be used because they are less readable, efficient, or prone to bugs. You can install it from here: https://jarl.etiennebacher.com/#installation
You might need to restart RStudio (or the IDE that you use, if you use one) after installing it. This tool runs in the terminal, not the R console. You can check that it is correctly installed by running jarl -V to print its version number.






Git: this is a version control tool, which is key in the software development process. It allows us to make and suggest changes to packages.
Github: this is the platform that stores the code for all of Palaeoverse. It also provides the interface to suggest, review, and implement code changes. Create a Github account if you don’t have one already.

You can check some of our workshop materials to see how to get started with Git, Github, and RStudio. Alternatively, the book “Happy Git and Github for the useR” is a useful, and free, resource. In this tutorial, we assume that you have already done these steps.
The remainder of this guide requires you to be familiar with a few Git actions: cloning, committing, branching, and pushing.

title: Contribute to our packages
text:
Get ready to contribute
You need to have an idea of what you want to change in the package. This could be a typo to fix or a new function argument to implement, among other things. You can take a look at all issues in Palaeoverse for inspiration. Note that almost all pull requests should refer to an issue (except for those that fix typos in the documentation for instance). If you can’t find an existing issue that discusses the changes you want to make, create one and ensure that making a pull request (PR) is necessary before opening one.
Once you have installed the tools detailed above and know what you want to do, it is time to fork and clone the relevant repository so that you have a local copy you can modify. You can then create a new branch that very briefly summarizes the type of change, e.g. “fix-typo-palaeorotate” or “add-arg-XXX-lat-bins-degrees”. Giving a readable name to a branch makes it easier to switch between branches in the future. It is also important to create a new branch early in the process so that we avoid pushing to “main” by mistake.

Once this is done, run pak::local_install_dev_deps() to install all packages used by this package (e.g. because they provide some functionality that is essential to the package, or because they help in the development process but are not strictly necessary for external users).
Before we start: contributing to an R package requires touching several files and understanding many concepts. It is absolutely fine to open PRs that are still work-in-progress and to ask for help where you are stuck. We are not expecting complete PRs from everyone.
Now that you have all development tools installed and created a new branch, you are ready to code!

title: Contribute to our packages
text:
Case study: “Improved binning for time_bins”
In this section, we will use an existing merged pull request as a case study to see the various steps in the development process. More specifically, we will use PR #131 (“Improved binning for time_bins”) of the palaeoverse package. You can open this link and go to the tab “Files changed” if you want to follow along. Note, this is a legacy PR and the function has evolved since this PR, it is only meant as an illustration for the contributing process.
The PR that we follow (“Improved binning for time_bins”) is a new feature: it adds the argument n_bins to time_bins() and improves this function’s performance. If you check the “Files changed” tab on Github, you can see that four files were modified:

man/time_bins.Rd
R/time_bins.R

tests/testthat/test-time_bins.R
NEWS.md

We will explain these changes in more detail in the following subsections.

Implement changes
The first thing to do is to run devtools::load_all(). This will load the current version of the package in the session. This is extremely useful because it means that you can easily test changes you make: any time you change something in the code, run devtools::load_all() to load these changes and experiment with them. For now, we haven’t touched anything, so this simply loads the latest version of the package.
At this point, steps to follow start diverging depending on what you want to do. If you want to fix a bug, you should first ensure that you can reproduce the bug in the current version of the package, before changing anything.
Here, the PR we follow is a new feature so we don’t have to test anything before starting writing code. In this PR, the bulk of the work is done in R/time_bins.R: this file contains the implementation of palaeoverse::time_bins(), and is where the new argument is implemented and where the code is modified to improve the function’s performance. This tutorial gives an overview of the development process so we will not go through all of the code here, but instead just highlight the major steps.






NoteAbout R packages’ structure



R packages follow a strict structure and should at least have the following folders:

R: contains all the R code related to the functions provided by the package. The function documentation is usually stored in the same file as the code (this documentation consists of comments starting with #').
man: this is short for “manual”. It contains the final documentation exported by the package. This is the content that we see when we do ?mean for instance. Files in this folder are automatically generated by devtools::document(), you shouldn’t modify them by hand.
tests: contains the tests for all the functions in the package.

Therefore, a pull request that improves the efficiency of a function but doesn’t change anything from the user point of view will only modify files in the R folder. Conversely, adding a new function or a new argument requires changes in R, man, and tests.




Ensure package-level robustness
Unlike when writing code for a research project, code contained in an R package must be stress-tested to ensure that users can only run it in the intended way. A key part of this is input error handling: these are checks that ensure that the values passed to our function arguments are appropriate for the downstream code.
Here, a new argument has been added to the function (n_bins), so we need to add error handling on this argument, specifically to ensure that a value has been provided, and that it is numeric.
if (!is.numeric(n_bins) && !is.null(n_bins)) {  
  stop("`n_bins` should be a 'numeric' or NULL.")  
}  
Crafting robust error handling is difficult! Start by thinking about what characteristics are shared by a range of appropriate values, and what would exclude inappropriate values. You can look at how other functions check inputs and how existing tests cover a variety of wrong inputs for inspiration. Ultimately we will include the error handling in our review process, so we can help you to ensure that inappropriate values are caught.
Note: after this PR was merged, we added some helper functions to make input checking easier, e.g. rlang::check_bool(x) to ensure that x can only be TRUE or FALSE.


Document changes
Depending on the changes you have made, you might need to add documentation or modify existing ones. Function documentation uses roxygen2. This means that you can modify the documentation in the same R file where you made changes (here, R/time_bins.R) and then compile it to automatically produce ‘manual’ files in the man folder (here, man/time_bins.Rd). Function documentation starts with #' in the R file. For instance, we can see that the docs for the new argument were added here:
#' @param n_bins \code{numeric}. For equal-length time bins, a   
#'   fixed number of time bins can be specified instead of a bin  
#'   `size`. This argument will be ignored if `size` is specified.  
Once you have made the required changes, use devtools::document() to compile the documentation. This automatically generates man/time_bins.Rd, you don’t need to modify this file by hand!


Test changes
If your contribution consists of fixing a bug or implementing a new feature, then you must add tests, i.e. checks that assess whether a function works in the desired fashion. This is necessary to ensure that the bug will not go unnoticed again in the future, or that the feature behaves as you expect, especially when future modifications are made to the package.
Tests are implemented with the package testthat. This broadly consists of two sets of functions:

test_that(...) is the general block where you define the name of the test (i.e. what this block is supposed to test) and where you write the code to test and the expectations it is supposed to match;

expect_*() are functions that help define what should happen. There are many expectations possible, e.g. expect_equal() to test values, expect_length() to test the length of an object, and expect_true() to test that an assertion is true. See the full list here.

You can find existing tests in tests/testthat. If you modified an existing function, then find the corresponding test file (tip: usethis::use_test() will open the corresponding test file). If you created a function, you should create a new test file. Here, the PR we follow added an argument to time_bins() so we need to add some tests to the existing file tests/testthat/test-time_bins.R.
You can run devtools::test() at any point in the development process to run the entire test suite. This is also helpful for finding bugs in new code, as it automatically flags when the code is not behaving as it should.
In RStudio, you can also use the button “Test” in the “Build” pane:

A good place to start is to try and throw errors from any new argument input error handling (and if you get an unexpected result, it’s worth revisiting the error handling). Looking at files changed in this PR, we can see three types of changes:

This PR modified time_bins() to print a message when the number of bins is automatically determined, so this existing test:
expect_equal(
  nrow(time_bins(interval = c("Phanerozoic"),  size = 25, rank = "stage")),
  22
)  
is now wrapped in expect_message():
expect_message(  
  expect_equal(
    nrow(time_bins(interval = c("Phanerozoic"),  size = 25, rank = "stage")),
    22
  )  
)  
Tests for the new behavior when it is expected to work:
# check that size- and n_bins-based bins are identical  
expect_message({bins_n <- time_bins(n_bins = 11)})  
expect_message({bins_size <- time_bins(size = 50)})  
expect_equal(bins_n, bins_size)  
Tests for the new behavior when it is expected to fail:
expect_error(time_bins(n_bins = 200))  

Note: this PR is slightly outdated in terms of coding practices. In particular, you should now use expect_snapshot(<code>, error = TRUE) instead of expect_error(<code>).
Your pull request will not be merged until the code is adequately tested, with all tests passing. In general, we aim for at least 95% of code coverage for new functions. Note that an automated comment detailing the coverage of your PR and indicating which lines are not covered will be posted shortly after you open a PR (you can also use the package covr to check this locally).


All the rest
We have now added a feature, added multiple tests, ensured that the entire test suite succeeds, and potentially added some extra documentation. We are almost done! But there are a few things left to do before opening a new pull request.
First, we should communicate our changes to the users (unless the contribution consists of typo fixes). This is done via the NEWS.md file, which contains the list of all changes that are relevant to external users (sometimes we make changes that improve the package but are invisible to the external users because they don’t change any existing behavior). Depending on your change, add a bullet point in “New features” or “Bug fixes”.
Second, we should ensure that our changes match the Palaeoverse standards in terms of code quality and styling. To do so, we can use two automated tools, Air and Jarl. As mentioned in the “Required tools” section, the former automatically formats code, and the latter automatically searches for bad patterns of code. Run air format . and jarl check . in the terminal (not the R console). Air shouldn’t error but it may happen that Jarl reports some errors, in which case you will have to fix them. It might be the case that running jarl check . --fix automatically fixes those errors.
Finally, run devtools::check(). This is a thorough checking function that includes devtools::test() but also runs a lot of other checks.
If all checks pass, you are ready to create a PR!


Make a new pull request
Commit all your changes to your branch, and then push your branch. On the GitHub repository, you should now see a yellow block suggesting to “Compare and open a pull request”. You can follow this button to prepare a PR.

You will need to add a title and a PR description. Prepare a concise description that explains the new feature or the bug fix. Note that if this PR is related to an issue, you can add “Fixes #[ISSUE NUMBER]” or “Closes #1234” in the PR description (not the PR title) to automatically link the issue and PR, which will also close the issue 1234 when the PR is merged.
Once this is done, you can open the pull request. This triggers a list of automated checks to run tests, check formatting, etc. Some of these checks will post an automated comment in case of failure, explaining the issue and how to solve it. If this is not the case, you will need to open their logs and investigate why they fail (feel free to ask for help if you cannot figure out the cause of failure).


Handle reviewers’ comments
Opening a PR is a big step, but it rarely is the end of the contributing process. You have spent some time on this PR (sometimes a long time) but package maintainers haven’t, and they may have some comments and questions that you will need to address. In the case of our example PR, the conversation contained more than 30 comments between the author and the reviewers.
After spending a long time on a PR, having a lot of back and forth with package maintainers can feel frustrating, even adversarial at some point. The Tidyverse code review principle is a very good resource to understand the various aspects of code review and to learn more about the reviewers’ point of view. In short, the following points are essential:

Don’t take it personally

Never respond in anger to code review comments

Fix the code

Think collaboratively

We all have the same objective: having good quality packages. Once your PR meets all code standards, passes all checks, and you have addressed all comments, your PR will be merged.
Thank you, and congrats!

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text: Palaeoverse was established in 2022 as a community-driven initiative dedicated to advancing open science through shared tools, training, and resources. To help ensure that our community remains inclusive and respectful, we feel that it is important to establish some expectations of behaviour when interacting within our spaces.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Scope
This Code of Conduct (CoC) applies to all individuals interacting in all Palaeoverse community spaces and activities, whether conducted in person or online. This includes, but is not limited to, GitHub repositories, Zulip channels, lecture series, workshops, meetings, and other community-sponsored events. In using these platforms, individuals confirm that they understand the CoC and consent to their behaviour being held against the standards defined in this document.
The CoC also applies to individuals when they are representing Palaeoverse or its community in public or professional contexts. Representation of the community may include, but is not limited to, the use of an official Palaeoverse email address, posting through an official social media account, or serving as a designated representative at online or in-person events.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Our Pledge
We as members, contributors, and leaders of Palaeoverse strive to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, irrespective of personal characteristics such as age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, marital status, parental status, or sexual identity and orientation.
We promise to act and interact in ways that foster an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Our Standards
Examples of behavior that contribute to a positive environment for our community include:

Demonstrating empathy and kindness towards other people

Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences

Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback

Accepting responsibility and apologising to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience

Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind

Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks

Public or private harassment

Publishing others’ private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission

Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Enforcement
Any conduct that poses an immediate or significant threat to the safety of individuals or the public, or that may constitute a criminal offence, should be reported promptly to the appropriate law enforcement authorities.
Instances of other abusive, harassing, discriminatory, or otherwise unacceptable behavior that contradict the terms laid out in this CoC may be reported to Pedro Godoy and Bethany Allen via the “Report Misconduct” form linked at the bottom of the Code of Conduct Page on our website. Alternatively, if the breach of rules occurs during an in-person meeting and requires immediate action, the incident can be reported (either by email or in-person) to one of the physically-present Palaeoverse team members. Where possible, individuals making a report are encouraged to provide any information or supporting documentation that may assist in understanding and addressing the concerns raised.
Anonymous reporting is available through the “Report Misconduct” form; however, it should be understood that this form of complaint may limit the ability of those responsible for reviewing the report to seek clarification, request additional information, or provide updates regarding the outcome. Anonymous reports will nevertheless be considered and addressed to the greatest possible extent.
Individuals who do not feel comfortable using the reporting form may instead contact members of the Palaeoverse Core Team directly via email. Reports will be handled as confidentially as possible, consistent with the need to investigate concerns and protect the safety and well-being of community members. All members of the community who receive reports are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Enforcement Procedure
All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly. Upon receiving the report, a meeting will be convened comprising at least three Palaeoverse Core Team members. If any Palaeoverse Core Team Member has a close professional or personal relationship with any of the parties involved, they should declare a conflict of interest and excuse themself from the meeting/decision making.
Meetings will aim to convene as soon as possible, and at least within 14 days of the complaint being received. If the complaint is made during an in-person event (e.g. workshop), the meeting should ideally occur on the same day as the report’s receival.
Once the Palaeoverse Core Team members present at the meeting have reviewed the complaint, they will determine whether any further information from the reporter and/or the reported party is required and will contact the appropriate party/parties to acquire this. Both parties should use this opportunity to provide any additional information they deem pertinent to the case. Once a decision has been reached, both the reporter and reported party (if previously contacted by Palaeoverse relating to the investigation) will receive written confirmation detailing any actions to be taken.
The reported party will be permitted to appeal the decision in the case of any new information coming to light. Once this information has been received, an additional meeting should be held by the Palaeoverse Core Team members, following the same timeline as laid out above for the initial report.
All Palaeoverse Core Team members retain the right and responsibility to immediately remove or reject written or spoken comments, posts, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned with this CoC without the need to convene a meeting. They will communicate reasons for their moderation decisions when appropriate. Consequences for the responsible party will be determined following a meeting of at least three Palaeoverse Core Team members. The party responsible for the breach of conduct will receive written confirmation detailing any consequences in line with our “Enforcement Responsibilities”.

title: Palaeoverse Code of Conduct
text:
Enforcement Responsibilities
Palaeoverse Core Team members are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will aim to take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.
The following guidelines will be used by Palaeoverse Core Team members in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

1. Correction
Offence: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.
Consequence: A private, written warning from the Palaeoverse Core Team will be issued, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. An apology to the impacted individuals may be requested.


2. Warning
Offence: A violation through a single incident, or a series of actions that have previously resulted in a correction.
Consequence: A formal warning will be issued, with additional consequences for any continued misconduct. The individual will be prohibited, for a specified period, from interacting with the people involved, including any unsolicited contact with those responsible for enforcing the Code of Conduct. This prohibition applies across all community spaces and external communication channels, including social media. Any violation of these restrictions may result in a temporary or permanent ban.


3. Temporary Ban
Offence: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior that has previously warranted corrections or warnings.
Consequence: A temporary ban will be imposed, prohibiting all participation, interaction, and public communication within the community. The duration of the ban will be determined on a case-by-case basis. During this period, the individual must not engage in any public or private contact with the people involved, including any unsolicited communication with those responsible for enforcing the Code of Conduct. Violation of these restrictions may result in a permanent ban.


4. Permanent Ban
Offence: An incident of gross misconduct, a pattern of violation of community standards (including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals), or breaking of a temporary ban.
Consequence: A permanent ban will be enforced, prohibiting all participation, engagement, and public interaction within the community.

title: AI Policy
text:
Palaeoverse is a community-driven initiative advancing open science in palaeontology through shared tools, training, and resources. Part of this initiative is to enable researchers at every career stage to learn and develop new technical and social skills. The human aspect of this work is therefore important to us and we are committed to maintaining spaces for human interaction and engagement. We acknowledge the potential usefulness and growing prevalence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), but wish to see it used only where reasonable and appropriate, whilst prioritising accuracy, accessibility, and upskilling.
The objective of this policy is to provide some guidelines regarding AI usage on our various platforms, such as Github and Zulip. This policy is adapted from Zulip’s AI policy.

title: AI Policy
text:
AI for communication
Do not post AI-generated messages: Zulip messages, Github issues, pull request (PR) descriptions, and other messages must be written by humans. If you need to quote an AI answer in a conversation, put the answer in a quote block (starting with “>” in Markdown) to distinguish AI output from your own thoughts.
You can use any tool you like for help with spelling, grammar, or translation, but ultimately must take personal responsibility for the messages you post.

title: AI Policy
text:
AI for coding
You can use any tool that helps you understand the Palaeoverse code repositories and write good code, including AI tools. If you used AI to generate code, you must disclose it in the pull request description and mention the tool and version used (e.g. Claude Opus 4.8, or OpenAI Codex 5.3). Additionally, you always need to understand and explain the changes you’re proposing to make, whether or not you used an AI as part of your process to produce them. The answer to “Why is X an improvement?” should never be “I’m not sure. The AI did it.”.
Do not submit an AI-generated PR you haven’t personally understood and tested.
Changes in documentation (e.g. documenting a new function argument, adding a vignette, editing the changelog) can be based on AI output, but it remains your responsibility to read through the entire text and ensure that it makes sense to you and represents your ideas concisely. It needs to be understood and appreciated by human readers. A good rule of thumb is that if you can’t make yourself carefully read some AI output that you generated, nobody else will want to read it either.

title: AI Policy
text:
Rule violations
Not following these rules will be treated as a Code of Conduct violation and will be addressed as detailed in the “Enforcement guidelines” section.

title: Join Zulip

Sign up to our Palaeoverse Zulip Workspace!
This is a space to interact with fellow palaeontologists, share useful resources, and post announcements for the broader palaeontological community.
If you are unfamiliar with Zulip as a communication tool, please refer closely to our personalised user guide. By registering to join this workspace, you are agreeing to follow the guidelines laid out in this document to the best of your ability. Detailed instructions for how to interact with the workspace are also provided in the description of each of our public channels. Please make sure to refer to these before posting. A more exhaustive guide on using Zulip, by the app’s developers, is provided here.
As with any community space, we feel it is important to establish some expectations of behaviour whilst interacting with other users. Therefore by registering to join this workspace, you are confirming that you have read, and agree to our Code of Conduct (CoC). Though the workspace enlists a dedicated team of moderators, if you personally suspect any breach of the rules, we kindly ask that you report these as soon as possible following the instructions provided in our user guide or via the methods detailed in our CoC.
We understand that at times, disputes are likely to occur in our workspace; however, it is expected that respect and professional courtesy are maintained at all times, and we encourage our users to read the following resources: How to Disagree Well.
